utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, everybody and good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Madam Tapuskovic, Mr. Nikolic. That's it, I think. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey on his own. The witness is already present. I take it that there are no preliminaries. No. In the meantime, Mr. McCloskey, there are two motions that I'm sure you are aware of from the Beara Defence team. We are shortening the deadline for the filing of the responses up until tomorrow. You can choose between filing a written response, or if you wish to respond orally at the beginning of the sitting or at the end of the sitting, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we have been discussing those motions and should be able to get back to you very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you, Colonel Vuga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Zivanovic, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, yesterday we spent quite a lot of time discussing the rules of service of security organs. I would only like to ask you one more thing. Who knew these rules of service? Whom were they intended? Was it for all members of the army or only certain categories?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of service are intended primarily for the service itself, to apply them in keeping with what is prescribed. And second, the rules of service are meant for all commanding officers who within their personnel have their security organs and command over them. That applies to the rules of service of the military police and the instructions for applying the rules of service of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at document from the Prosecutor's list, 2741.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the English text is on the screen. You can see that this is an instruction about command and control over the security and intelligence organs of the Army of Republika Srpska dated 24 October 1994. First of all, could you tell us what does "instruction" mean in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An instruction in military terminology is a regulatory document which instructs as to the procedures of those to whom the instruction applies. It can have a binding nature depending on what weight is attached to it, so it can be either binding or it can serve as a pointer, as a guideline. So this particular instruction on command and control applies to those who command and control over security and intelligence organs, and in the substance of the text there are stipulations as to what those to whom the instruction applies must be guided by. That's all the commanding officers and commanders who within their units have security organs and intelligence organs over whom they exercise command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, can this instruction be considered as a new enactment relative to the rules of service for security organs or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These instructions in keeping with the rules of service of security organs determine the way the rules are going to be applied, but it does not stipulate how particular affairs will be conducted in security organs. It doesn't go that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify a bit? In which way does it determine ways in which the rules of service for security organs will be applied?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions reflect needs that arise in the specific circumstances in which the VRS was active. It was a very special set of circumstances. I don't need to emphasise that, but let me point out the following: In view of those needs, these instructions imposed on the military leadership and the Main Staff that they should guide security and intelligence organs in such a way as to be able to efficiently protect the army, especially in the area that relates to counter-intelligence because that was one of the greatest problems they faced, at least according to the evaluation given in the introductory part of these instructions. Let me also emphasise that these instructions underlined one set of problems that are related not only to the activities of security organs but also other issues that have an impact on security organs and have an impact on their activities and their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, in which way does this instruction govern this distribution of time that security organs should devote in their work to those affairs that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its contents, these instructions established a certain relationship between counter-intelligence affairs for which security organs are responsible on the one hand, and on the other hand affairs in which security organs participate in their commands; that is, staff and command, military police and proceedings preliminary to prosecution. The instruction determines that 80 per cent of all the work load of security organs should be focused on counter-intelligence, whereas 20 per cent of their capacities should be devoted or spent on affairs in the other three areas in which security organs are participants. This ratio is approximate, like, reflected by the study preliminary to this instruction. In our study, this ratio was considered to be optimal. If security organs are 85 per cent engaged in counter-intelligence, then in this instruction it is 80 per cent of their overall engagement. I have reason to believe that the circumstances and the situations in which the security organs in the VRS were active dictated this more stringent ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 2 of these instructions, which says that the security organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit of which they form part; but with regard to professional activities they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organ of the superior command. Can you explain exactly what this is supposed to mean, controlled centrally? Can you make this distinction between the powers of the commander and this centralised control by the security organ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a foundational objection. The previous question he said "I have reason to believe that the circumstances ..." Could we clarify whether that is because of his study as an expert or that -- does he have some actual personal experience on the ground or in the field at the time that would give us some idea of how to view these answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a very fair comment. Mr. Zivanovic, will you please ask the witness to address these issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuga, let us clear up the point raised by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I was trying to answer briefly so I did not expand on what I said, I have reason to believe, but I will explain what reasons they are. A study was made, and I compared it -- I compared this text to the study that preceded the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just speak more slowly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule was written and the study was made in peacetime, in regular conditions. That is, at the time when developments occurred in relatively stable conditions. The intelligence activities focused on activities that jeopardised the security of the Yugoslav People's Army and the armed forces, and they took place at a time when there was no armed conflict, there was no war. And even then, the findings of our study indicated that 75 per cent, around 75 per cent - this cannot be quantified precisely, but it can be presented as a ratio - 75 per cent of time and work was devoted to counter-intelligence work. That was satisfactory to counter secret threatening activities. My conclusions about the circumstances in which the armed conflict and the civil war took place of the nature they had in Bosnia-Herzegovina compared to the findings of our study and the documents I studied and which I evaluated for the degree of threats and the shape of threats to the VRS, all that led me to say I have reason to believe that this percentage in those circumstances from the viewpoint of engagement of security organs had to be increased compared to the situation in the JNA, in the SFRY, in those past conditions. That is the substance of my conclusion, and that is the basis of my position. When I say I have reason to believe that this led the author - that is, the Main Staff of the VRS - to act in this way with regard to the command and control over security and intelligence organs of the VRS, of course, that applies also to intelligence organs. That is the full answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify your answer. When you say to increase the engagement of security organs, on what part of their work was their engagement increased?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily on the greatest threats. At the time when this paper was written, at the time of the study and the rule, we did not have incursions by sabotage terrorist groups. If there were any, they were negligible to what they were like in the war. In the rules of the brigade, there is one provision that says that combat against Special Forces in addition to counter-intelligence work by security organs shall be led in other ways. This is just one illustration of the extent to which the circumstances and the situation changed in wartime for security organs as opposed to peacetime. So that is the substantial difference. Furthermore, it almost needs no explanation what other things the war brings for security organs. Even everyday life is changed in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, let me come back to the question I asked before. That is, could you clarify paragraph 2 of these instructions? What does it mean that security organs with regard to professional activities are controlled centrally by the superior security organ, by the security organ of the superior command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question you asked, Mr. Zivanovic, points out the existence of strictly professional affairs that we discussed to some extent yesterday, which have certain common needs and common features at all levels of command in the Army of Republika Srpska, and in order to be efficient, they have to be linked up into one functional whole, which is able to provide a fast flow of information within that whole, its appropriate and full evaluation, and quick response in situations where professional work could have the best and the most efficient results. So centralised means that in one place, almost simultaneously all the information about threats flows in, important experience is identified that may be important to the whole system, and that experience through feedback is given to all the vehicles of counter-intelligence affairs, and all officers in position wherever they are can count on it that this experience will be available in their area, in their location. And they in their turn whenever they get information that could be important to the whole system make it available to the system as soon as possible, as quickly as possible, so that there is sufficient knowledge about the threats to Republika Srpska at all levels. This way, the command at the highest level can make decisions and distribute assignments to subordinates in keeping with its overall knowledge and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this same paragraph, there is reference to the independence of security organs in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and operative combinations. You explained to us what counter-intelligence tasks mean. You can perhaps explain in a few words what intelligence task means, but tell us, what is operative combinations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "operative combination" is a very complex term speaking of the structure of the task that needs to be executed, but I'll try to explain it in simple terms. Security organs have at their disposal or, rather, it is prescribed for them, that they can apply a total of 11 methods of work individually or in a combination. So if a source provides a report that somebody is suspected of working for a foreign intelligence service and that a move needs to be made towards an interesting or a potentially interesting contact, it depends on the source what we are going to do next. And then the choice has to be made of the method which will be used for that follow-up activity, and that is a combination of these methods that should lead us to knowledge that will provide the answer to the question, what kind of threat are we dealing with? That's one aspect of operative combination. Another aspect, which is not just the privilege of security organs or intelligence organs of the VRS, this is applied by all services and it's based on their experience, and that is the following: Through persons who are located in an area which is of interest to the intelligence service, they should try to create a possibility for collecting information on the enemy side, legally or otherwise, and bring that person over to our side, also providing them with appropriate cover and a legend as to why they were on the enemy side and then on our side. Another task in this respect is to find persons who are fit for that task, whether it is in the domain of intelligence or counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not having translation, basically. I don't know what's happening. I waited a bit, but it went on too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuga, the independence of security organs as defined under item 2 of this instruction, does it go beyond the framework that have been laid by the rules of service? Does it redefine this independence in a new way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The independence is not redefined here. It is just pointed out and made more prominent so as to put it in the focus of those who make decisions on the tasks of the security organ and when these -- the execution of these tasks is controlled. I've already explained the nature of these tasks, but let me go back to them and say the following: The independence in the choice of source of data and independence in the choice of a combination that will be applied when executing a task reflects in the fact that nothing can be foreseen in advance. You cannot choose a specific person. That's why you have to spend some time seeking a proper solution. It cannot be said in advance that some intelligence activity has been discovered. That's why you need a process and a combination that will lead to that. That is why this -- these data and this manner of work cannot lead to a conclusion that would lend itself to an immediate solution. A question may be asked whether what is beyond the control and command by the nature of its development and occurrence really belongs to the function of command when you take into account the element of strict confidentiality which is prescribed and which has to be complied with. So these are the reasons for which the independence is necessary, for which it is prescribed, and for which it has to be complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to item 3 of this instruction, which is page 2 in e-court, both in B/C/S and in English. This part of the instruction speaks about the duty of the intelligence organ to inform their immediately superior commanders about their evaluations and observations. You have already told us how this is prescribed in the rules of service of the intelligence organ -- security organ, but can you please tell us whether this is laid down in the same way in this instruction, or maybe there are discrepancies there.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part, the instruction is very consistent in the application of the provisions of the rules of service, and it just underscores both for the commanders and the security organs the fact that this application -- obligation cannot be ignored because it is of a major significance for the one and the other. That's why it is emphasised here that in security organ is a member of the command and that the data available to the commander- and I'm talking about assessments, conclusions and proposals at -- which they have arrived in their counter-intelligence work - should be made available to the commander of the unit and to the organs of the command when the commander does not need those directly. That's why the instruction is consistent and has not changed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Item 4 of the instruction speaks about reporting on the part of the security organ along the professional lines to the security organ of the superior command. Since this part of the communication is defined as a state secret in this part of the instruction, would you be able to tell us whether this is consistent or not with the rules of service of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, we looked at item 25, which points to the fact that there are limitations in terms of reporting on one part or, to be more precise, on the data which refer to the methods used by the security organs in their work. This is in keeping with the rules of service and the instructions on the application of methods in the work of the security organs. Actually, just the methods of the security organ because the application is something that the security organs do. So there are no specific requests. This particular request can be found in the rules of service in a somewhat condensed form, both in the domain of command and control and the domain of the collection of data by the security organs, the only difference being the fact that this has been rounded up as one unit and highlighted in a way for everybody to see better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this item, a special emphasis is put on the telegrams and mail sent by the members of the security and intelligence organs. Tell me, please, is this part in keeping with the rules of service of the security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of service does not deal with the matters of mail. The rules of service deals with the data and the significance, and manner of their conveyance is only a way to make them available to those that they intended for. As far as this part is concerned, it speaks about the specific manners of conveyance, and the ones that are mentioned here are just some of the ways data can be transmitted in a protected way, or -- so as to prevent leaks. A telegram and -- telegrams and mail are mentioned because under those circumstances this must have been or probably was the most common way of establishing contact because other ways of transmitting data were not that readily available. All the transfer of data has to be -- had to be treated in that way, and the data had to be protected in the way mentioned herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 5, a reference is made to the personnel policy in the intelligence and security organs, also reassignments, sending people to special tasks and so on and so forth. Could you please again answer whether this is in consistency with the rules of service or whether there are any aberrations from those rules?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of service has laid the functional determination as to what the security organs will be dealing with. The person in command and control of the organ of security in totality was duty-bound to apply the rule and find personnel and organisational solutions in order to implement the rule by applying certain criteria for the personnel that will be responsible for the execution of some tasks. And this is not the only criterion that was valid in the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska that was used in selecting staff. There were other checks for other positions in the Army of Republika Srpska. According to the rule for some positions which are listed in the rules, there is a mandatory vetting procedure. I spoke about the personnel in the security service which apply here when it comes to their removal, transfer, the disciplinary measures, and so on and so forth. In this particular instance, the commander was not powerless. There was a line of command and control with various levels at which all of these issues can be dealt with. In other words, a decision should have been made in keeping with the overall status of the function of the security organ and the work of the security organ in that function. There was one part which was carried out in the command, and there was another part which was part of the counter-intelligence that was professionally guided by the higher organs of security under the full control of its legality, professionalism, and efficiency; and this made up a whole, and that's why it was determined in the terms of the personnel that this should be done in the Army of Republika Srpska in keeping with the rules. Hence, these items of the instructions, which are in consistency with what has been determined by the Main Staff of Republika Srpska when it came to the performance of duties of the security organs as well as in the other spheres of work and activity of different organs of Republika Srpska. It is not in contradiction with the rules. It is in keeping with the function and role of the commander of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. And this is given in the rules in items 95 and 96 and in the authorities which were given to the commander of the Main Staff. Obviously, this has been translated because we don't have a single document that would exclude any of the items from the rules. Hence, the authority is in consistency with what can be found in the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your answer, page 13, line 25 of the transcript, you said that the commander was not powerless. Could you please expand and clarify? What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant what it actually was. A commander had his security organ and gave him tasks which did not rely only on the methods of work. His participation in all that when it came to the realisation of measures of security, his command and guiding the military police [as interpreted], his participation in the precriminal procedure, and now I can mention a number of other issues that the security organ in the command was involved in. In those issues, the situation is clear and it is absolutely clear that the security organ was absolutely responsible for the security of his unit, and in those terms some of the tasks that he had within the counter-intelligence sphere, he tied as much as possible and resolved as much as possible within the authority of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have an error in the transcript. Actually, in the interpretation. Line -- page 15, line 4, where the witness said that in his professional guiding of -- and command of the military police, which has not been entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Professional guidance, not command of the military police. The interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I can continue. I've been interrupted. I would like to continue providing my answer at the place where I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. And the interpreters, please or whoever will be looking after the transcript, make note of the correction that Madam Nikolic has indicated. Check it. Do you agree with what Madam Nikolic has explained to us or not, Mr. Vuga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That was absolutely correct. Professional guidance of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you can now proceed with what you were saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me also say this: In that respect, the commander has the full authority over the security organ with some limitations that said that taking measures against the security organ, any measures, be it reward or punishment, disciplinary measures, promotion, or any other measures that were available within the sphere of command, either in connection with the full knowledge of the 85 per cent of his work in counter-intelligence jobs, and then that decision could be founded on realistic foundations. If that had not been the case, the most important part of the function would have been ignored, and decisions on the work of the security organ would not have been valid, and this is the essence of all these determinations with just one more remark, something that I spoke about yesterday, and this is the criteria that were applied for the selection of personnel for the security organ, and those criteria were in the hands of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And this could not be interfered with at any level without the knowledge of the person who signed those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me move on to para 7 of this instruction. I believe it's on the next page of both the English and the Serbian. It says that the monitoring of the professionalism, legality, and correctness of the work of the security and intelligence organs shall be carried out exclusively by the first superior organs for security and intelligence affairs except in that part of their engagement which relates to command and staff affairs. Can you just clarify, looking at this instruction, is this in keeping with the rules of service for security organs that we discussed before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is consistent with the rules of service for security organs. It's not only consistent; it makes a clear distinction between technical, professional affairs, and the monitoring of that where the commander does not interfere, and even the superior organs do not have much influence on that part of their work. It says except in that part of their engagement relating to command and staff affairs. So nobody else has the right to control or monitor the security organ in that area. The vertical chain is hereby distinguished. It does not fall within the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one part of your answer, where you say that even the immediate -- even when -- that even the superior organs did not have much impact on that area.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. They have no impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the security organs or the superior command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the monitoring of professionalism and legality of security organs in the area of counter-intelligence work. The very beginning of the sentence determines the issue, and that is where the separation line lies between the area performed by the command. You don't tamper with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The monitoring of professionalism, legality, and correctness of their work regarding command and staff affairs, can you tell us again who does this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This monitoring is in the exclusive purview of the commander. The commander decides on the proposals of the security organs, how well he reports, and how well he participates in the evaluation of security, et cetera. The commander is the only person who can decide about that and undertake everything and anything that is at the disposal of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do security organs of the superior command have any influence here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instruction rules that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And let us look at paragraph 8, as well, because you said that the instruction is two-pronged. Can you tell us from para 8 what is the impact and the consequences of these instructions in a specific case?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instruction is explicit when it comes to complying with its contents and the persons to whom it applies. It leaves no open questions as to what to do and how to implement it. Strict compliance with this instruction is required. Even the word "strict" is included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you also studied the instructions on the methods and resources of security organs, and you told us that there were 11 such methods. I'm not going to go through all of them. You've already explained a number of them sufficiently, such as working with a source or running a source. Just tell us about the first method. That is document 3D275. In B/C/S it's page 8; in English, it's 9. I'm sorry. B/C/S, it's page 5. In English, it's 8. The first method listed under number 1, we see counter-intelligence evaluation. 3D275, page 8 in English. Can you tell us what it means, counter-intelligence assessment or evaluation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The counter-intelligence assessment by a security organ is a method defined here and should have been and was implemented in practice. It was consistently applied. It is a constant process of mental and practical activity. It is continuous, uninterrupted, within the purview of the security organ, and the objective of this activity is to evaluate on the basis of available information threatening activities and the sources of threat and our own forces for countering these activities, that is, the security service and various security organs distributed across various levels; and to produce a conclusion as to the balance of power between these two sides and what is needed to improve this balance of power to the benefit of protection of one's own security. In this respect, every new fact that is learned that indicates that something needs to be done triggers again a new counter-intelligence assessment and evaluating whether this new fact makes us -- puts us in a better position or in a worse position and what needs to be done to counter this threat. That is the preliminary element, a sine qua non, an element without which we do not know what measures to take. And it says as a basis for any other activity in the sphere of counter-intelligence. That is the substance and the meaning of the counter-intelligence assessment. There are other things that needs to be said, but they belong in the strictly professional domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify, when you said it is a permanent, continuous process, a continuing obligation and duty, in what sense is it a continuing obligation of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to make a comparison that should illustrate the meaning of the word "continuing" in this sense. A guard, a sentry who was assigned to secure a facility or installation is under obligation to constantly guard that installation and prevent anyone who wants to put it in jeopardy. The security organ is constantly on guard with his counter-intelligence assessments. He must not miss a single fact, occurrence, or development when we are talking about countermeasures beginning with the first indications of threat and going up to the centres and sources of this threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In point 11, which we see on the screen in English - in B/C/S it's on the following page - we see a list of activities monitored by the security organ. Tell us, is this counter-intelligence assessment subject to modification, and if so, in what intervals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a living organism and it changes constantly, from the viewpoint of counter-intelligence work, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could that mean that it changes on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can change minute by minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us at great length about methods of running a source. I'm not going to ask you any more about that. But tell us, is that also a continuing task for security organs or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All methods of work that are applied independently by the security organ are continuing. They are equally alive as the counter-intelligence assessments. They constitute a special symbiosis in the sense that there can be no change of counter-intelligence assessment without a new piece of information, a new situation, a new fact; and equally, one cannot successfully run a source and apply methods of work unless we can draw conclusions from the counter-intelligence assessment about the next step, the follow-up method of work, and the next solution. So these two are closely intertwined and condition each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In response to my question, you said that all methods of work that the security organ applies independently are continuing. Now, tell me, with regard to the 11 methods listed in the instruction, which are the methods that the security organ applies independently?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first four. The first four on the list in the instruction. That's counter-intelligence assessment, running a source, interviews, and gathering information and fact-finding. Those are the first four methods of work for which the security organ does not need to request approval from his superior. When I say superior, I mean professionally superior because this is a purely professional, technical part of its work. That is consistent with all the other rules, regulations, and laws, that there should be no interference with the security organ's work where he needs to make decision. I mean wiretapping and recording, secret checks, and inspection of mail and other things. This means that I can run a source independently following the procedure that I explained yesterday as to how a source is recruited and how a source is run. All these same issues are the same when it comes to control by a superior professional organ, professional management, et cetera, in interviews, et cetera. The obligation is continuing for the security organ to regularly report to the superior security officer so that the superior security officer has full insight into his work, that he can provide guidance, and evaluate whether the lower security organ is working properly or if he is either overstepping the -- his authority or violating some other regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you could just clarify one term that we often encounter here. What is an "operative action"? That's on page 26 in B/C/S and 32 in English of the same document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the rules of service, we have operative processing as a method of work of security organs for detecting, monitoring, and countering enemy threatening activities directed against the Army of Republika Srpska, whether they are directed against the army from outside or from inside. An operative action, unlike operative processing, is the most complex and the most extensive form of engagement of all security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska. Whereas in operative processing the security officer runs the assignment and performs it as instructed, in an operative action all security organs of the VRS are engaged. That means that there has been a serious breach of security of the VRS or a serious breach of security of some vital point of security that all security organs are under obligation to protect at all costs wherever they are in keeping with the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I might have missed something, but if you could remind me of the document which deals with the 11 methods of security organs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is this directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you show me the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 8 -- 18 -- 8, sorry, page 8, in English. And document is 3D275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the e-court can show the document to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can go very fast through the document, through all 11 methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no need for that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have it? A, B, C, D, E?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. We are at counter-intelligence assessment. It is just first method of counter-intelligence -- for all counter-intelligence methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me be clear. So counter-intelligence assessment is number 1 of the 11 methods?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we haven't seen all those 11 methods. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I now understand it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can move on to page 12 in the B/C/S and 9 in the English version. The second method, running a source. We have been discussing this. I won't have any questions concerning that, but we will just go through all the methods. The next method is gathering and assessing information, page 5 in the B/C/S -- excuse me, page 9 in the B/C/S and page 9 in the English. No, it seems not to be. Page 15 in the English version. The fourth method is interviewing, page 10 in the B/C/S, page 16 in the English version or, rather, in the English translation, excuse me. The fifth method, disinformation, is page 17 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what page it is in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sixth method is covert surveillance, page 15 in the B/C/S, page 17 in the English. The seventh method are covert searches, page 16 in the B/C/S, 19 in the English. The eighth method is wiretapping and interception, page 17 in the B/C/S and 20 in the English. The ninth method is secret checks of mail, page 18 in the B/C/S and 22 of the English translation. The tenth method is analysis, page 19 in B/C/S and 23 in English. The eleventh method, research, the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, would you clarify for us a term described at page 27 in the B/C/S and 33 in the English. "Counter-intelligence protection": Can you tell us what it's about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One needs to say the following: Counter-intelligence protection can be viewed as overall activities of security organs in the domain of counter-intelligence because it is all for the purpose of counter-intelligence protection of the armed forces. However, this one was singled out as a separate task because it is believed that out of all of the objects protected, some of them will be under a particularly grave threat. In order to prevent such a threat in as organised a way as possible, in order to protect the objects efficiently, as one of the jobs and tasks of the security organ in -- within the framework of combined methods of work, counter-intelligence protection is aimed at particular objects that are to be chosen according to the level of threat and level of importance. In keeping with that assessment, a decision is made to provide counter-intelligence protection for such objects. That should be distinguished from the general term of counter-intelligence protection. However, this one refers to the most important objects. This is separately ordered by a superior, prescribing the methods to be used and prescribing who is to be acquainted with the work of the security organ in terms of counter-intelligence protection of the specific object as part of the specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question concerning this document: Is there a mention of POWs anywhere in the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, item 134, where sources are referred to there is a mention of POWs as sources of information when these are members of Special Forces, which may be of particular interest to security organs in terms of collecting data. The security organ is duty-bound to detect the activities of such troops in the area they are responsible for, including the facilities in that area. There is no other mention of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the methods, although I said I wouldn't be asking you any questions concerning that, but please, comment the fourth, continuous method. You mentioned this being the interview. Could you please clarify it for us and tell us what it exactly entails. It is page 10 in the B/C/S and 16 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interviews as a method of work of security organs could be compared to interviews as existing in other professions. The difference, however, is that these are secret interviews unavailable to other professions and domains. They are target-oriented, limited to such persons who may be in possession of security-related information. Information needs to be gathered on whether there is enemy activity which may be of interest for the security organ as well as to include everything else that can be found out for the security organ to embark upon its counter-intelligence assessment. Interviews are conducted with the persons who are estimated as being of interest and who may be willing to assist the security organ in completing its tasks. These are not sources but people for whom the security organ assessed that may be of assistance. That method of work is very widespread. One does not expect particularly quality information from such interviews but certain indications pointing in the direction of where one should focus its work and when one can expect to come across good cooperation. These people are supposed to provide cooperation in the work of the security organ. How should I put it? This is a very across-the-board, brush stroke-type of communication aimed at a large front of gathering data and subsequently processing it in order to arrive at a right assessment in that domain, which is the topic of the interview. There is something else I need to add to it. By virtue of such interviews, one gathers the most information concerning the general state of security. That general state of security points to certain creaks, weaknesses, through which a danger or threat may arrive. Frequently, it enables the security organ to paint a picture to the commander concerning the situation in the unit on the issues which just border on the counter-intelligence domain. That's the gist of the method and ways of conducting interviews. These are covert ways of communicating. Such persons providing data are protected, and this is applied generally to persons who may provide such information which is not open and available to just about anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To clarify, are such interviews conducted only with army members?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the term "persons." There are conditions to be met in order to have such interviews with persons outside the unit. So it says here "persons." Therefore, it is not restricted to army members only, but it is the most practical to do it with soldiers because they are in the same environment. However, it can also include persons in the territory or persons occupying such job posts that may have access to certain information. There are numerous possibilities for conducting such an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, do you believe that in clarifying your report one needs to address any other issues from the instruction, save for or in addition to those I've asked you about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we should.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of everything said, there are three important things to be borne in mind. The methods of work of the security organs are covert ways of gathering information. It applies to all of the methods and all of the information as well as all of the persons providing information. The second part of it is this: The methods of work of the security organs include covert ways of processing data. What does it mean? When processing data, there is a very strict number of persons who may be acquainted with what is being processed. The third part of everything that was said so far is this: The methods of work of the security organs are covert ways of using data. All information users in relation to the information itself are determined selectively according to certain criteria. Every person can know things to the extent needed in order to perform his or her functional duties or to the extent of what he or she needs in order to implement a task. Anything beyond that is not permitted. That is the entry and exit delineating the space in which the methods of work of the security organs can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we make a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will have the break now. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuga, I would like to move to the rules of service for the military police that you also dealt with in your expert report. This is P707. First, let me ask you -- page 7 in B/C/S and page 8 in English, and I'm speaking about the rules of service for the military police, P707. First of all, could you please tell us in very general terms and very briefly, what is the military police? How are the military police defined by the rules?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is defined as specially trained and organised units which perform military police tasks. This is not just any ordinary troops or people performing combat tasks in the units. Those are especially selected, specially organised and trained units that perform military police tasks. According to the rules, they have everything that is intended for these units to have, which is equipment, organisation, professionalism. In other words by norms, organisation and education, they are intended for the military police tasks which they are entrusted with by law. I have been too fast, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You should slow down, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 5, which is on the following page in the B/C/S version - the English page remains the same - it arises from this item that a certain sort of selection is carried out for the replenishment of these units. Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke yesterday about the criteria and the selection process, I said that there were authorities given to the persons in the security organs. These authorities are also given to the individuals in the military police to use weapons. They are independent in their decisions to use weapons. One of the reasons for the selection process is to decide who will be able to decide independently on the use of weapons in combat. The second reason is the character and nature of tasks performed by the military police in peacetime under the immediate threat of war and in the conditions of war, which differs from other tasks performed by the military and the military organisations. The difference lies in the fact that they have to apply law in the areas which are not in conflict with the enemy side in terms of being engaged in combat directly but, rather, they have to institute the regime of safety, maintain the regime of safety and security, protect facilities, control the area and amongst other things, they have to conduct combat and fight against the infiltrated sabotage enemy units whose activity is aimed at threatening those facilities under the protection of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now explain for us under item 1 of this rule -- can we please go back to the previous page in the original B/C/S text. The English text is before us, the same as before. It says here amongst other things that the military police perform certain security jobs. Since you've already told us that the security organs also perform certain security jobs, could you please make a distinction between the two groups of jobs, the security organs on the one hand and the military police on the other hand? Can you please explain the difference between the two groups of jobs and tasks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we have already spoken at great length about the security organs and their tasks, unlike the security organs the military police within its purview deals with the tasks pertaining to the area of general security, which means that in this domain the security tasks do not contain the elements of fighting covert enemy activity, and they don't apply those methods of work as applied by the security organs, save for those that are prescribed for the -- for fighting crime and acting upon performing certain jobs in terms of providing technical security of the facilities. Everything else is a relatively classical manner of action within the domain of security, and they perform those tasks by performing prescribed duties and services.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to command and control of the military police? This is page 8 in B/C/S and page 10 in English. I apologise. It will be page 9 in B/C/S. It says here that the officer of the military unit is in control and commands over the police -- military police unit on its strength. What is the meaning of the word "commands"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Controls the military police unit. The interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I could ask Mr. Zivanovic to tell us which B/C/S word you used in asking this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Rukovodjenje. [Interpretation] Control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe this has been translated as command, but this is not the -- what I wanted. I didn't want you to explain the term command but the term "control." What does it mean to control a military police unit? Now this has been interpreted in a different way, but it is another issue. Anyway, can you please explain the meaning of the term "to control" a military police unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "control" in the military police has the same significance as the term "control" in military units, in other spheres of activity, not only in the sphere of security but in other spheres as well. I'll try and explain the meaning in very broad outlines. Control is a planned and organised activity aimed at preparing, organising, enabling, and equipping a unit to perform its tasks. This would be in the most general terms, which means that a commander who commands and controls a military police unit which is on its strength has the powers, the obligations, and the responsibility which is -- with which he is entrusted with regard to the activities comprised within the term of "control." I believe that I have been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us very briefly, if you can, what does the term "control" imply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term implies the fact that the commander has a unit whose purpose is prescribed by this rule and that the commander has this unit under his command within the framework of its intention. It has to be prepared and organised and be capable of doing what it is supposed to do to influence. He has to control, command, and influence the unit to be ready to perform its tasks. When he makes a decision that, the unit has to act upon his decision. He does that in keeping with the organisation and establishment structure that he has in his command in the unit that is intended for the purposes relative to the military police. He doesn't have to do everything in person, but it is part of his responsibility to deal with the issues, and he has the powers of the commander within his commanding role. So this is practically this part of activity, i.e., it is within the authority of the commander to do this when it comes to the military police. In practical terms, that is that. I could tell you more about the unit. He has to be reported on the status of the unit. Within the status of the unit he can order some corrective measures that have to be undertaken in order for him to take control over this, to see what is the difference between the task given and the task accomplished, what is the difference between the mission given and the mission accomplished. There is a number of things that the commander has to know in order to know the status of the unit that he commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you this: How do you effect control over the military police unit? I.e., how does one control the performance of the tasks; how do you check that the unit has accomplished the tasks given to it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we explained the part that concerns the professional control of the -- over the military police unit. We have to make a connection between the professional control and the command over the unit, and we have to separate one from the other. Actually, we have to tie one to the other and establish -- and separate one from the other. The security organ is the professional organ for the tasks of the state security in the command. He has the broadest knowledge within that area, and based on that knowledge he can assess the threats and those who pose that threat, and he can also assess the ways and manners to counter the threat in the way most efficient to protect the unit. Since the police acts within the domain of the protection of the unit and its -- and the safety of facilities, people, and technical means and everything else within its purview, and the organ of security does the same only using other methods. That means that in one part of the protection, countering the enemy is the common foundation for the assessment, conclusion, and evaluation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. He's going so fast that I think there is misstatements and mistranslations. He's talking about state security. So I think it may benefit all if he would slow down, and you may want to see if that's a correct translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the most practical way to go about it is for me to read out the question and he to start giving his answer again. Forget about what we have between lines 12 and 25. Please answer the question again, Colonel Vuga, and try to speak as slowly as you can, please. The question that Mr. Zivanovic put to you was the following: "And now I would like to ask you this: How do you effect control over the military police unit? That is, how does one control the performance of the tasks; how do you check that the unit has accomplished the tasks given to it?" Could you please answer that question going slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more question by me. Out of curiosity, the English word "control" in this set of question and answer is a translation of "kontrola," not "rukovodjenje." I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is -- there is no consistency in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted the consistency in transcript. "Rukovodjenje" is translated as in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And here we see "control" without inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. My question is regarding "control" as "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I observed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me consult my colleagues on something which is related to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and if anyone is not able to follow, please let us know. Colonel, do you want me to repeat the question to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how the word "control" was translated to the colonel from your question, as "rukovodjenje" or as "kontrola." I do not follow it in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't addressing him. I was addressing you. So that's not a problem. The important thing is that since we are following in English, I wouldn't know unless I have the inverted commas whether you're using "rukovodjenje" or "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Judge Prost is referring me to the question that I read out, which was your question, and we would like to know when I used, how do you effect control over the military police unit, and then how does one control the performance, what word was used by the interpreters in translating my English into B/C/S. Did you use "rukovodjenje," or did you use "kontrola"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I used "kontrola," B/C/S word "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I am not receiving an input. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to complicate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But in none of the -- if he's referring to the regulations and all that we've seen, we see the word "rukovodjenje." It doesn't mean the term "kontrola" is not relevant, but it certainly is going to confuse the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honour. Let me just answer your question. You asked how the interpreters interpreted when you used the word "control." In B/C/S, we heard "kontrola." So for "rukovodjenje," the witness heard "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I understand that was the word used by Mr. Zivanovic himself. In putting the question to Colonel Vuga, according to Mr. Zivanovic, he -- for "control" he didn't use the word "rukovodjenje" but he used the word "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my last question. In previous question, I used word "rukovodjenje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, let's proceed. Have you been able to follow what we have been discussing, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I followed very carefully, and I believe I understand what is being asked of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Then proceed with your answer, please, and move slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kontrola, monitoring, is one of the functions of command, one of. Monitoring means that the commander has full information about the status of the unit and all the things that are relevant to its function, as opposed to what was set as an objective of control, and to establish discrepancies between what has been achieved and what was set as an objective. So compared to the task, the objective, what was achieved in practice. That is monitoring or inspection. Based on monitoring, further measures, follow-up measures, are taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us with regard to a unit of military police, who in fact does the monitoring of its performance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The monitoring instead of -- in the sense of assessing the status, as has been said, is done on behalf of the commander by the security organ as a technical, professional organ for monitoring professional guidance and other activities over the military police because this is a technical job, a professional job. It's not generally military so much as technical in terms of organising, enabling, and equipping the military police unit in keeping with its profile as defined. The security organ reports to the commander about the results of the monitoring and the inspection that the commander needs to carry out over the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in addition to security organs and those professional elements, is monitoring done by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit of the military police has its own commanding officer who directly commands his unit. He is duty-bound to report to the commander about the state of affairs in his unit and everything else relevant to the military police unit within the system of command, within the framework of commanding a military police unit. So under the system of single command, the primarily responsible person is the commander of the military police unit who has operative command. He monitors the performance of tasks and reports to the commander. This answerability to the commander may be direct or may be effected through the security organs. This is on a case-to-case basis depending on how it is decided to effect command and control over the military police units. I used the term "command" now because the whole system of controlling is directed towards command. That is assigning and performing tasks. That's the only reason a military police unit exists, to be given a task and to perform it. Everything else is subordinated to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the commander of the unit within whose composition the military police unit is, does he monitor, does he have the powers to monitor the execution and the performance of this military police unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit commander has the right to monitor every unit subordinated to him in all aspects. That includes the military police. There are no exceptions. Here we are talking about the professional component, which is dominant in establishing insight into units. That's the reason why the security organ is involved as the professional organ of the commander for controlling military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now go back to point 7, para 7, of this rule? It is on page 8 in B/C/S and page 9 in English. It says here that military police may not be used for performing work outside its own requirements and assignments, save for the army commander or some other highly placed military commanding officer. Tell me, what is the situation if a military police unit is used for assignments that are not envisaged by the rule of service of the military police? First of all, who would be answerable for such a use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using a military police unit outside its purview, outside its prescribed tasks, requires special procedure, which means that approval must be requested from the competent commanding officer. That would be here the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. He must be asked to approve to use a military police unit outside its prescribed tasks. If situations occur when the military police is used for assignments that fall within the area of expertise of combat units, a chain of command, a chain of jurisdiction exists, in place, how that would be done, and the commanding officer has to act accordingly. Let me use an example. If in the VRS there is a general order or a general approval from the commander of the Main Staff that military police may be used in combat activities on the front line together with other units of the Army of Republika Srpska, then the decision fell to the commanders of units who had military police on their strength because such a general order existed that the military police may be used in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about the professional management of military police units and professional monitoring of their performance. Tell me, did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Zivanovic. Are you leaving this item 7? Para 7? You're done with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering, in addition to the commander, this paragraph provides that an equal or higher ranking military officer also is able to give authorisation. So, Mr. Vuga, if you could tell me the meaning of this phrase. Who are they referring to, an equal or higher ranking military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meaning of this term lies in how the military police is defined together with its function and task. That is to avoid situations where military police units would be used too frequently or irrationally. Therefore, this decision, how to use these units for certain tasks, is given to the higher ranking commander depending on how the needs arise. That is because the military police in view of its training and capacity is a very suitable unit for use in various tasks which fall outside its area of expertise. To avoid resorting to this kind of use of military police units, it is required that approval must be sought. It is an entitlement of a higher-ranking officer to decide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can give me examples of such equal or higher-ranking military officer who can give such authorisation for the military police to be used to perform duties outside their needs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can use the example of combat operations. In territories where combat operations took place, problems sometimes occurred that needed to be dealt with from the segment that begins with roads being cut off as a result of military destruction, military police could be used for such assignments. It's not strictly within its purview, but it can be used for that purpose. But in that case, a higher-ranking officer has to decide whether the assignment is of such a nature that military police can be taken away from its regular duties and whether they can be spared for that amount of time in order that the military police can deal with the emergency assignment, so to speak. That is a matter of assessment. The officer who makes the decision takes that risk upon himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us now, since you described professional monitoring and general monitoring over the performance of military police and its use, what are obligations of security organs in professional monitoring of military police units when they are used outside their prescribed assignments, outside their prescribed scope of work as defined by the rule?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can say one thing immediately: When the military police is really military police, and when does it go beyond that function or outside that function? As long as military police is performing its duties within the prescribed scope of work, they are acting as military police. When military police go outside of that function and perform some other tasks, including the example I've just given, then the security organ can no longer professionally control the military police because the expertise for such use of the military police lies with the person who suggested such use and who will implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You dealt with the next point quite sufficiently in your report, but could you tell us some more about the scope of work of the military police? That's on page 11 in B/C/S and page 12 in English.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The jurisdiction and the scope of work of the military police are precisely defined by this rule. They relate to security provided for the purposes of the Army of Republika Srpska in wartime, and it was the task of the JNA and the Territorial Defence, but that's not the way it functioned in the VRS, in Republika Srpska. You have security provided to areas, persons, installations, detection of crimes that are prosecuted ex officio before military courts. It also includes security provided to military officers when required, protection of documents of the highest degree of confidentiality that are of significance for the defence of the country. So those are the main tasks for which the military police is engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the scope of work or its tasks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are both the scope of work and tasks of the military police. The military police is in charge of security and security jobs, both its scope of work and its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. I would now kindly ask you to tell me, within the framework of the military police tasks, how do we go from the tasks to the service of the military police? This is 17 in B/C/S and 20 in English.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the tasks that are prescribed by the rules of service the military police realises by performing the services of the military police. It is prescribed for the military police to perform seven different types of services through which it carries out the tasks. These services are prescribed by the instruction on the application and use of military police. This instruction elaborates the ways how the rules of service are implemented. The instruction, therefore, elaborates the services of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus on two of these services. I would not dwell upon each and every one of them. The first one would be the security service that you have on the screen before you. I will kindly ask you to tell us briefly what this service implies.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service is actually the most voluminous service that the military police is involved in. It comprises several actions and tasks which are in the function of performing the security service that the military police is entrusted with. The service's task is to provide security for the object of security, which may be persons, facilities, military data, and everything that falls within the scope of work of the military police and its tasks. When it comes to the security service, the substance is to prevent access, incursion, or any other threat to those things that are secured by the military police and to acquire the level of security for anything that has been determined. I don't mean just anything but all those things that are designated as objects of security. It may be the command post, the officer. In other words, the security service comprises everything that should not fall under any threat, and that is the object of security. This is the essence of the security service, which implies all sorts of things that have been incorporated into the security service. Those are patrols and other services that are incorporated into the overall security service in order to achieve the goals and objectives of this security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for gesturing. I just wanted to warn you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understood. I may be a little bit slow on the uptake, but I certainly understood what you meant by your gesture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at page 19 in B/C/S and in page 20 of the English translation, and the service that I'm interested in is the so-called escorting service. Actually, it is 21 in English. This is paragraph under number 4 at the very bottom of the English page 21. It should be 19 in B/C/S. Yes. That's it. Item 54 speaks about the escort service, and here a reference is made to people deprived of liberty. I'm talking about items 54 through 57. In the English version, it will be on the following page, and the same applies to the B/C/S version. So can you tell us something about people who have been taken into custody? Actually, were prisoners of war mentioned under item number 55? Could we then hear from you something about this service in particular and more specifically about prisoners of war and people taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that the escort service applies to people and property who are secured from the moment of reception to the handover to the bodies in charge. The essence of this escort service is in providing security. In the following paragraph, it says that the military police carry out escort service upon an order by the officer in charge of the military unit, also applies to prisoners of war, but one thing has to be noted here. This is when the authorities request that. An authority that may request escort is determined inasmuch as being able to make decisions on the command and use of the military police, and he may be requested to issue an order for some prisoners of war to be escorted. This is elaborated in the instruction on the use of -- on the application of rules of service, which provides further instructions about the request and a decision upon this request. One thing has to be noted here. Prisoners of war are not included in the regular tasks of the military police. They are given as a possibility that a body in charge will issue a request and that the military police will act upon the decision or the request. If a request is issued, it may be approved or not approved, so this is given as a possibility for the military police to perform such tasks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in addition to this provision, is there anything in the rules of service for the military police, any other provision that regulates the issue of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a provision according to which within the security service the military police provide security for prisoners of war in the prisoners of war camps and participates in escorting them from the division stations for prisoners of war to the places designated for them, which may be a prisoner of war camp. In other words, the military police participates in these tasks. In a camp, it provides security for the prisoners of war or the inmates of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now kindly ask you to move to the next document, which is the instruction on the application of the rules of service of the military police. This is 3D276. Can we please look at Article 18, which is on page 10 in B/C/S and on page 2 of the English translation. In this text, in paragraph 18 of this text, it says, "The commanding officer of the military police makes a proposal to the superior military commander directly or through the security organ of the command staff unit and institution of which the military police unit is part on the use of the military police for carrying out duties and tasks falling within its range of responsibilities." Tell me, please, is this what you were talking about yesterday, about proposals to use the military police? Is this what you were talking about?
