Is this the norm that provides the basis of the commander of the military police unit to propose the way it's going to be used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Colonel. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading. "Is this the norm."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who gives proposals for the use of the military police unit in accordance with this rule?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to be more specific when talking about the term "command" over the military police use because in principle, a single command means that a commanding officer proposes the use of his unit because he is the one responsible for the performance of the unit's tasks and the security organ, and he proposes that to the immediate superior or through the security organ as it is stated herein. And now we come to the two proposals that need to be very clear. The first proposal is the proposal of the commander of the unit who is in command of the unit and is responsible for its overall status and the performance of its tasks. He is the best suited to know every single individual in his unit and based on that thorough knowledge and the thorough knowledge of the unit, he formulates the proposal and submits that proposal to his own commander. The security organ whose role has already been explained in the unit has additional information about possible threats against the object of protection, and based on his professional knowledge he assesses the proposal of the commander of the military police unit and provides the proposal with the part of professional contents which he as the person best informed and privy to the security matters can propose, can draft, and then he makes an integral proposal from the professional point of view on as -- on how the military police unit should actually be used. The unit commander based on the proposal submitted to him has ample or might have ample elements in order to make a decision based on thorough and full information from the purview of the commander of the military police unit and from the purview of the security organ, and then he will be able to draft an integral proposal for the protection of unit, which falls under the scope of objects protected by the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now clarify your answer? Because in two places you mentioned the unit commander, and in one situation you said that the unit commander issues a proposal and in another situation he decides on that proposal.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we have a problem. We have commanders of military police battalions, and we have a commanders of military police companies, and I may have not been precise because I was talking about the battalions on the one hand and the companies on the other hand. So that's one part of the problem that concerns the military police in purest terms. And when I was talking about the commanders, I omitted to use the word "The commander of the military police unit." I have not explained myself thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he's the one who submits his proposals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's his task. That's one of his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to refer to item number 255 on page 49 in B/C/S and on the same page of the English translation, the same page that is already on the screen. This provision also talks about escorting POWs, so I would kindly ask you to tell us, what are the specific characteristics of this provision as opposed to the provision quoted just a little while ago from the rules of service for the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This provision falls within the escorting service and provides very clear guidelines as to what obligations does the military police have in escorting POWs, what is determined as a possibility in the rules. It is here stated how this should be done. The activity itself is worked out in a rather great detail here. Now, the escorting techniques and the manners of escorting are not the essence -- of any essence for us here, but there are some indications about the escorting of the POWs. They refer primarily to the fact that when a military police unit is assigned to escort POWs, according to this instruction this military police unit is assigned to escort more important POWs, which implies that those are persons or POWs for whose security in escort there is a higher degree of interest, hence a higher degree of obligation, and then there is also a procedure regulating the escort of such POWs that goes from making a list to the handover. There are a lot of things that I wouldn't like to dwell upon. What matters is the fact that the persons, the military policemen, i.e. the unit in charge of the escort has to be fully informed of all the details of their task by the person who issues the task, who requests this escort, because the essence of everything is in the request, what has to be realised when the military police is given the task of escort of POWs. There is also a part of the regulation which says that the military police participates in the escort of POWs, i.e. it not only escorts the more important ones but also participates when this is specially requested. I have to emphasise that the issue of participation is the matter of assessment. When we talk about participation, a possibility is given to the officer to assess the justification of the request, and based on the justification of the request he can decide to have the military police engage, and this is a more closer determination of what is stated in the rules of service. By this, a task is given to the military police to act according to all the principles and requests that have to be complied with in the escort service when prisoners of war or any prisoners are escorted. There are different things here. For example, it would be good if somebody spoke the language of the prisoners of war, different procedures that are prescribed to be undertaken in various cases that may occur during the escort service, and one more part that is important to know, the security organs in their professional management of the military police, in the part that concerns prisoners of war have an obligation to, if they are aware of something that might put the whole assignment under risk, should point to those risks to the commander. They have to point to the threats, and they have to propose measures to him to enable him to react and remove that threat or prevent that threat with a view to a successful accomplishment of the task. The security organ is not a higher authority for the escort service. The best-suited people for that are the military policemen and the unit in charge. However, they need additional information if such information exists, which will allow them to understand what needs to be done in order to accomplish the mission to the end. They are duty-bound to receive a signature on the piece of paper proving that they have accomplished the mission, and on their return they have to brief the officer who has ordered the security service and to tell him how and when the mission was actually accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain something? You said that the military police can participate in the escort of prisoners of war. Does this mean that somebody else will be in charge of such activities? And if that is the case, could you please tell us who that person or body is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it is somebody else who is in charge, and it also means that I have to go back to the reasons why somebody else is in charge to explain things better. First of all, very rare situations in which military police takes prisoners, prisoners are taken where combat takes place, on the front line, on the separation line where prisoners of war appear as disarmed enemy soldiers who have fallen under the authority of, first, the unit that took them and then the force that this unit is a part of. This means that the first part of escort is something that has to be done by the unit who took the prisoners of war, and then in depth as they go further away from the combat area, they are gradually taken over from one place to another where they are finally going to be collected. This happens at the divisional station, and I'm quoting from the rules in order to explain things better. When the military police, who is professionally equipped for this task and when the number of prisoners is higher, they will participate together with the unit to help them. In professional terms, the military police never do it on their own, but their professional capabilities will help the unit who has captured them to do their job better. This is the term of participation in that part. When this comes to the person in charge, then it will be the unit with its troops starting with the company commander. There is an instruction which describes the level at which the issue of the treatment of prisoners of war is dealt with. This was issued by the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska in July 1992. And in this instruction, it says that the responsibility starts with the company commander. The company doesn't have a military police unit, and the next place will be the battalion. That will be the place where prisoners of war are collected and there, as well, there is no military police. And then it is necessary to deal with these matters at the level of the brigade command that has a military police unit, and they have to participate in that. Now, this is the term of "participation" that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? Sorry, but I couldn't make the witness stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting on this important topic. I just -- there was an interchange of the terms "in charge" and "command," if that would be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, you probably heard the Prosecutor's remark. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would need to learn more about where the misunderstanding lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If the Prosecution has the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. It was in the beginning of the answer, and he said that the command was in charge several times. And it may again just be a translation issue, but is this unit in charge or in command or something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in the first line. That's line 18 on the previous page, page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out the part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is that even your question was translated by the use of the words or the phrase "in charge." In you look at lines 14 to 17, particularly line 16, you'll see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is part of my question, it seems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I don't know because I'm following in English, not in B/C/S. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. Please tell us briefly, you said that the military police takes part in the escort of POWs, which means that somebody else should -- is the principal player in that process.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were about to arrive there but the longer way, the longer route. The instruction sets out that the main entity doing that begins with the unit which had taken prisoners, and its commander, and then vertically along the line of command up to the highest-ranking organs which are to decide the fate of the POWs. In other words, it means that the line of command is used starting from the company upwards. In that sense, the -- that's where the care of POWs lie. The commander of the unit which has military police as a part of it decides at a certain moment of the POW escort and guarding in the police stations decides on the participation of the military police, and I've already explained the notion of the term "participation."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me next, in order to clarify your report even further, do we need to focus on any other part of the rules of service of the military police and the instruction we have analysed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief to be able to understand what the essence of the topics discussed so far. There is this -- the professional aspect of security in any given unit, which comprises basically all elements in terms of threat assessment and actors of the threat as well as all the elements which are used to counter such activities. That's the professional component. It also, of course, includes assessing information, making conclusions in that domain. Another part is the operational capacity and purpose to tackle the issues from the security domain in which we have organisation, education and training, professionalism, and capacity to react. All these factors are adjusted with a view to performing a function. The security organs are one entity and the military police another entity in the field of security. If their joint goal is to protect a unit, they still have divided competences and tasks as well as capacities. In that way, each of them can be active in their respective domain with a clear profile. The security organ from the point of view of security domain professionalism are those which are the professional organs assigned to any command. That's why we have difficulties because the operational aspects of a task are sometimes unnecessarily carried by the security organ. That is not the point. There is an operational organ within the unit under the unit's command, whereas the security organ, if there is a need for a unit or an individual to implement certain tasks, that individual or that unit can do that in terms of engaging the military police but only following an approval. Otherwise, no tasks could be assigned to any military policeman or to the military police unit because that type of work lies exclusively with the unit commander as regards the military police and the commander of the unit as regards his unit. That's what I thought was necessary to explain from everything we have said so far in terms of relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A clarification, please. You said that the security organ -- or rather, that the security organ is a professional organ dealing with threat protection. Could you please be precise? Are these secret threats, all threats in general, or something else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organ for security as part of its command carries out threat assessments. Such threat assessments encompass all types and means of threat, and the security organ is there to collect information on those. Once that is done, the security organ proposes to the command what to do, and the security organ takes participation in that, and in its own security assessment the professional part belonging to the security organs is taken apart, is taken out. If in the course of a security assessment the security organ concludes that the threat involved is of greater size but, however, still does not have any clear and visible data, based on the assessment used as a platform to make an assessment on the overall security that security organ also needs to participate in the collection of data with the command to see what they have on their part. Then that is put together, and together with the counter-intelligence assessment the security organ talks to the commander, explaining the level of threat from the point of security. The function of security reached the conclusion that the unit's security is endangered to this or that level or extent. And then the command needs to take up that part, and the security organ follows up through its own professional line in terms of security aspects alone, professionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, another thing: We are quite interested in how the security rules we have been discussing were applied at the corps level. What rules in the VRS regulated the work of the corps of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the VRS, the rules of service of the corps land forces was in application. That was the rules that were applied. One can see that from the various combat and operational documents, and there were no other rules in place. The army was established according to the rules per tasks. The corps was established in a way that it was visible from the rules that it had been established according to the rules themselves with certain adjustments. The rules provide for a general framework as -- but real-life situations and practice do not make it possible to always implement the rules to the fullest. However, in general, the rule was -- the rules were in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a Prosecution exhibit, which is P412, next. We can move to page 181 in the B/C/S and 110 in the English. The English text is fine. In the B/C/S, we should skip two pages forward. It should be 183, I believe. That's it. Mr. Vuga, in your report you also took into account security regulation. That is in your second binder. Please go ahead and find that in your documents.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the rules in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 468. It begins with item 468 and then carries on, and I meant paragraph 468, not page 468. As regards to the rules of service, are these security items which you had occasion to analyse, do they truly and accurately reflect the provisions of the rules of service for security organs which we have discussed? Were those rules reflected in these rules?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the rules of service of the security organ, in terms of army security those provisions put in simplest words were distributed across or into various rules in keeping with the level of units that they were supposed to be applied in. That's why we have a situation, then, that whenever a security organ is involved, its role is defined as part of the command depending, of course, on the level of command. Its tasks and duties and its range of responsibilities stems out of the rules of service of the security organ, this being the basic document defining everything that has to do with the range of responsibilities of the security organ and its tasks. When one looks at these rules, we always have to refer back to the rules of service of the security organ and the military police rules of service, which are decisive when the application of these rules that we have before us are concerned, in terms of security and the application of the rules of service of the military police and security organs. When you studied the rules of the corps, you always have to refer to the previous rules. There are no inconsistencies, only the definitions were changed and applied to the corps level in terms of command, cooperation, and everything else done at the corps command. Anything that is important for the functioning of the security organ of the corps command is included therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 468, first sentence, it says, "Security support is a type of support in operations and other combat actions which is based on a system of security and self-protection in the corps established earlier in peacetime." When it says, "In the corps," does it encompass the entire defence area of the corps or only the corps command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see that this includes the whole of the corps and not the command alone. That means that it is the area of responsibility of the corps, and the command is of course at the head -- at the helm of the corps. Within this context, however, security issues are tackled by the corps command and its organs, and the area involved is the area of the corps where the corps was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to item 3, which is in the B/C/S on the next page and in the English, we can see it on this page, but it carries over to the next page. Among other things, it says that this includes timely organisation and implementation of counter-intelligence measures and activities, these being detection and prevention of secret organised activities of foreign intelligence services, activities and actions of reconnaissance, sabotage, and terrorist forces, activities and actions of special units of the enemy, activities of enemy emigrants, and internal enemies. Does that mean that the corps security organ needs to take care of all these things, as it's stated here, in a timely fashion, in order to detect the aforementioned activities throughout the area of defence of the corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ, according to this definition which has been adopted from the rules of service of the security organ, but here it has been adapted to the corps, is duty-bound to organise all this and to implement all this in the corps. Obviously, that's why he has a certain structure which will be able to realise all this, but he is responsible for everything that will be done in the corps as the person in charge of the counter-intelligence function and tasks as their organiser and professional manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have to leave it at that for the time being. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just briefly, I wanted to inform you that the Prosecution has no objection to another opening statement from Mr. Ostojic. We would like to continue to speak with him on all the other matters this afternoon as we have been speaking, and I think after that tomorrow morning we will have a better idea and be able to tell you more information then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you while doing this kindly remind him that he hasn't filed a revised complete 65 ter list, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will certainly. Yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Let's proceed. Mr. Zivanovic, you'll need to wait for the witness to come in. Where are we? Halfway through?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuga, we were discussing paragraph 468 of the rule of the corps that deals with the organisation and implementation of certain measures, and now I'd like to move on to 469, which stipulates types of tasks that are implemented in zones of operation and are placed within the framework of security support in the corps. Let us look at the first two points because my next question will focus on them. That is, counteraction to and prevention of activities of foreign intelligence services, reconnaissance and sabotage units of the enemy, special units, activities of hostile Yugoslav emigration, and the internal enemy. And point 2, protection and direct security of the system of command and control and communications, commands and units of the corps and the units of Territorial Defence acting in concert with them, protection of sensitive and vital structures within the units and in the operation zone, protection of the secrecy of decisions, plans and combat documentation. Now, does this also pertain to the entire zone of defence of the corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of it pertains to the entire zone as written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, tell us, is it possible in times of war that these tasks not be performed by anyone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible because the purpose of the corps as a unit would be called into question, and then this element of security of executing tasks would be absent, and the tasks themselves could not be executed in the absence of the prescribed measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at one more document, a regulatory document. That's an instruction for the work of commands and staffs, 699, P699. [In English] Page 109 in B/C/S and 100 in English. [Interpretation] It's an instruction for the work of commands and staffs. Let me first ask you, was this instruction applied in the Army of Republika Srpska as a regulatory document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documentation that I studied, I concluded that this instruction was applied. I concluded that because in various documents I found elements of orders and provisions which can be identified as compliance with this instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 222, the second paragraph of this item, which is on the next page in English. It reads, I'm only reading the first sentence, "Security measures must be continuous and functionally organised." In the context of this provision, could it happen that these measures failed to be implemented for one or more days within the command of the Drina Corps in the course of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question could boil down to a comparative analysis whether there was an interruption in threatening activities when the command of the corps could rest and not take any steps to secure itself. The continuous character and functional organisation of security measures depends primarily on the continuity of threatening activities which were also uninterrupted and targeted the whole system with the aim of destabilising it and endangering its function. That means the whole system of command, command posts, systems of communication, et cetera. So if this is implemented consistently, it could not be interrupted, not for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, do you believe from the viewpoint of your report anything else needs to be said about the rule of ground forces or this instruction that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of the rule of ground forces, we discussed the segment that is part of what I studied. It provides answers, although not detailed, to what we have been discussing, a bit more than what I wrote in my report, but this needs to be said. I think we need to note that with such extensive tasks as we have here in the zone of the corps, a certain organisational structure needs to be in place that has the capacity to perform these tasks. The tasks themselves as defined tell us that these are very complex, very extensive, continuous tasks. That implies adequate human resources, a high degree of professionalism on their part; they must be equipped properly for these tasks and have the capacity to perform them within the time they are given in such a way as to enable the whole system to function securely. There are two terms that are used at a level of needed security and at the level of set security. One element is the security that provides safety to those who are executing their tasks, in peacetime, in wartime, and in circumstances of immediate threat of war under the specific circumstances of each of these conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before we conclude the examination of these documents that are covered in your reports, what is the practical meaning of security support and security specifically at times of war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aspect of security that we are discussing is the function of security organs and the professional security service. It has a special importance in wartime because enemy activities and threats as a whole directed against commands and units of the corps are implemented usually covertly with small forces in order to maximise the effects and to achieve an effect of surprise, both in terms of the objective and in terms of method. Therefore, the system of command and the corps as a command must have at their disposal the staff, professionally trained, organised staff and resources, in order to achieve maximum success in executing these tasks. Therein lies the importance of security support. As for the consequences of not implementing these measures, they are usually very grave and irreparable. They cannot be removed quickly, and redressing the consequences requires a lot of time and great efforts, and it's usually too late. That's the importance of this provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to discussing combat documents that you analysed in your report, I'd like to go through certain regulatory documents enacted by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time and just before, documents which should reflect the general situation and especially the security situation in this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you please take the third binder in your set, and take document 1D710. This is an enactment of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 4 April 1992. In item 1, you see that a decision was made by the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 3rd of April, 1992, to carry out a mobilisation of Territorial Defence units. First of all, tell us, do you know whether this decision was taken by the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in its full composition or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the documents that I analysed, the Presidency was not in its full composition when it took this decision. The representatives of the Serbian people in the Presidency, those who represented the Serbian people under the constitution, were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify what this term "Territorial Defence" meant in that system? Who was comprised by Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was an integral component of the armed forces of the SFRY. JNA was one component as federal army, and the Territorial Defence was another component of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the requirements, who had the obligation, who had to be a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Territorial Defence were citizens of the SFRY who were not in the JNA, who were not doing their military service, but who were of military age and able-bodied and who had the obligation to be members of the Territorial Defence of the territory of the Republic in which they had wartime assignments and in which they resided. The whole thing was governed by the constitution. It was stipulated in the constitution what the Territorial Defence was, who was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Take it slowly, please. In item 3, there is a reference to the mobilisation of the reserve force of the police of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you specify what was the reserve force of the police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reserve force of the police was within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior. It doesn't infringe upon the Territorial Defence and the jurisdiction of military authorities. That is a separate plan and a separate type of implementation of that plan. I did not deal with this issue in particular, but I know from my previous jobs what the reserve force of the police means. I knew what sphere they worked in because in my various security-related positions I had some insight into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at document 1D1282. Could we lower the page. This is a decision to proclaim an immediate threat of war. Can you see when it was taken?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it was taken on the 8th of April, 1992, signed by the President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, if I made the right connection because it's on two different pages in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we move to the second page? Here we see the signature, but we moved to this page to look at another decision that is closer to the bottom of the page. It's the decision to introduce the work obligation. Can you tell us, from what you know, what does "work obligation" mean under circumstances when an immediate threat of war has been proclaimed as we have seen from the previous decision?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work obligation as explained here in the context of these developments and under the legislation implies that introducing the work obligation will create the prerequisites and introduce an obligation for layers of society to whom the work obligation applies will act in a new way as opposed to before, and that these segments of society will function in accordance with the state of immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see from the text that the work obligation is entering into force for all the state authorities, public enterprises, self-employed businessmen, banks, republic and municipal organs of administration. So as far as I can see, no one is left out.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that these agencies are explicitly included, but I don't know what it took to include other elements. Perhaps there is an aspect that could ensure that the work obligation and the work performed be in the interests of security, so it is possible that not everything is encompassed by this provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to relevance, and for the first time the witness appears to be speculating. He's saying, perhaps, I don't know, and this is not something I see in his report, and it's really not like him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think the witness has heard what you just said and will avoid doing that in the future. In the meantime, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now look at 1D731. This is a decree on defence. This is a decree Law on Defence. Could you please tell us when this decree law was passed and by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree law was passed by the Presidency on the 17th of June, 1992, according to the document, which is signed by President Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I -- I believe that you are looking at a wrong document, or maybe we have made a mistake. The number is 1D731.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decree law was passed by the Presidency. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I have is a -- the decree Law on Defence bearing a different date. That's why I'm saying that you may be looking at a different document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it's not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you can look on the screen if that's not a problem. Maybe it will be better. Can you see in the right upper corner? Let's blow it up just a little bit for you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 20 May 1992, but I was looking at the date when the decree law was passed, not when it was published. It was published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 20 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was going to ask you. Now I would like you to look at Article 48 of this decree law. It is on page 3 of this document. Kindly look at the definition of the age limits for the work obligation that I've just asked you about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The age limit for the work obligation is from the age of 15 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at Article 50 on the same page, which defines the age range for the civilian protection units.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The age range for the civilian protection units is between 80 to 60 years of age -- I apologise, between 18 to 60 years of age. This is for men, and 55 years of age is the upper limit for women.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, can we please look at Article 51, which is relative to the training for defence. Could you please, again, give us the age range when it comes to rights and obligations for training for defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the range is between 15 and 60 years of age for men and between 15 and 55 for women if they are fit for training. So the main conditions are fitness and age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to a different document, which is 1D729. I believe that's the one that we saw just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I haven't objected but just going to documents and having him read out things really is more time-consuming than probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's true. I mean, if we can avoid that. You know, in practically all the domestic jurisdictions that I know, that is an anathema.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have an objection to him citing that information and asking it in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 1D729? And can he tell us whether the state of war was ever proclaimed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if it was, when was it proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state of war was proclaimed on the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same document, could you please look at an order and tell us what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to this document, the essence of this document refers to the proclamation of public mobilisation, which is binding upon all citizens between the ages of 18 and 65 who are fit for service and women between the ages of 18 and 55, to report to the units of civilian protection where they will be assigned duties to perform. And also, this is a call for general public mobilisation of all militarily able men between the ages of 18 and 55 who are to report to their respective military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The order in paragraph 1, does it prescribe what military conscripts have to bring when responding to the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated very clearly that they should bring military equipment and personal weapons and that they should report to the nearest unit of Territorial Defence. The mobilisation implied that they should come with all the gear that is envisaged to be brought to a Territorial Defence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D712 -- 1D720.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decree law on military obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- I apologise. Let's just wait for the document to appear on the screen. Could you please tell me the date of this decree law?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. On what basis is he saying that this is -- goes back to the 1st August, 1992? Because what I see in front of me here on the monitor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because he looks at his binder and not on the display. It is wrong document on display.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. That explains it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It could be displayed on ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to look at Article 2. This is the sole provision that we are concerned with. Could you please tell me, according to this decree law who falls under the military obligation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the provisions of this decree law in Article 2, in both peace and war, all the citizens of Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina who are fit for service fall under the military obligation. This is the basis. And later on, there are conditions which are subsequently prescribed and arise from this decree law, but the general provision and condition is fitness for work, and it also says here that the responsible persons are companies, institutions, and other legal persons, and their organs and other legal persons. The important thing is that part of the obligations that have to be carried out are also binding upon the structures of society who have been tasked with implementing duties within the area of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Fauveau. One moment, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we maybe be a little more clear on lines 13 and 14 in 1970? It says that it is the citizens of Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it Republika Srpska, or is it Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a correction which has not been recorded. I said, no, I misspoke, it was -- it is Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this has not been recorded, the fact that I corrected myself, and this is probably due to the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about this. Tell me, if you remember, do you remember the lower age limit for the work obligation? How young can a person be in order to fall under the work obligation provisions? If you can't remember, let's go back to the document to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can go back but the lower limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The relevance of work obligation in 1992? I mean, what -- this is going to be a long war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance, and then we close it there because it's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because -- the relevance of it because the working obligation starts at 15 and military obligation starts at 15, as well, according to this rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take that up. I will take that up tomorrow, until which time we stand adjourned. We start at 9.00 sharp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
